children: Naveen Jindal says shortages in skilled trades could push wages higher as employers increasingly compete for job-ready talent

Jindal Steel is stepping up workforce training as it confronts what Chairman Naveen Jindal describes as a significant shortage of skilled workers, with demand for vocational talent potentially driving higher wages in the years ahead.

Speaking on the sidelines of the WorldSkills Competition 2026 in Shanghai, Jindal said the company was placing greater emphasis on continuous training to address the skills gap. He said the skilling effort would now be expanded substantially as industries increasingly need workers with practical, job-ready capabilities.

Jindal argued that demand and supply could increasingly determine earning potential across occupations. He pointed to trades such as carpentry, plumbing, electrical installation, air-conditioning and refrigeration, saying shortages of capable workers in these areas could make such jobs more lucrative.

His comments also challenge the traditional emphasis on university degrees as the primary route to employment. Jindal said not every young person needs to pursue higher education or become an engineer or doctor, arguing that vocational skills can provide routes into employment, entrepreneurship and overseas opportunities.

The focus on practical skills comes amid wider efforts to strengthen India's vocational workforce. In April, the Ministry of Steel launched industry-linked skill development courses for ITI students and shop-floor employees in the secondary steel sector, citing a shortage of skilled manpower and the need for more practical training.

Jindal Steel already runs Dakshata, its company-wide skills development programme covering technical mastery, workplace safety, functional and behavioural training and leadership development. Its NEST initiative is designed to assess contractual workers for role fit, safety awareness and job readiness at the point of onboarding.

For HR leaders, the discussion points to a changing equation between formal qualifications, employability and pay. As manufacturing and other sectors expand, employers may increasingly need to build talent pipelines through ITIs, apprenticeships and continuous workplace training rather than depend solely on graduate recruitment.
The shift also puts skilled trades back into the conversation around career choice, at a time when employers are facing shortages in roles where hands-on expertise can be difficult to replace.
